solution:
**Waxes** — the high molecular weight (higher, solid) alkanes.

This chapter's list of uses of alkanes says it directly: "Waxes are high molecular weight alkanes. They are used as lubricants." These are the alkanes at the top of the series; the chapter notes that alkanes from about 18 carbon atoms onwards are solids, and that those with more than 35 carbon atoms (tar) are used for road surfacing. The same waxes are also used for making candles and carbon black.

**Ethene** (ethylene), \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH_2}\).

The chapter's list of uses of alkenes says that ethene and propene are used to manufacture polythene and polypropylene, which find use in bags, toys, bottles and so on. Polythene — the polymer of ethene — is the material of polythene bags, so the alkene asked for is ethene.

**Benzene**, \(\mathrm{C_6H_6}\).

The chapter's section on carcinogenicity and toxicity of benzene states that benzene is both toxic and carcinogenic (cancer causing), and that it "might be considered the mother of all carcinogens", because so many carcinogens contain benzene rings. In the liver benzene is oxidised to an epoxide, and these substances can react with DNA and induce mutations leading to uncontrolled growth of cancer cells.

**Crude petroleum (crude oil) and natural gas.**

The chapter's section on the industrial preparation of alkanes says that crude petroleum and natural gas are the source of alkanes. Dead plants buried under the earth billions of years ago were converted to crude oil under high temperature and pressure; the oil collects in dome-shaped cavities called oil wells, and the individual alkanes are separated from it by **fractional distillation of crude oil** in oil refineries.

The three isomers of \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\), in **increasing order of boiling point**, are

**2,2-dimethylpropane < 2-methylbutane < pentane**

| Structure | IUPAC name | Common name | b.p. / K |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{C(CH_3)_4}\) | 2,2-Dimethylpropane | neopentane | 282.5 |
| \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3}\) | 2-Methylbutane | isopentane | 300.9 |
| \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\) | Pentane | n-pentane | 309.1 |

The boiling points are those printed in Table 15.2 of this chapter, and the order follows the reason the chapter gives: all three have the same molecular formula and the same molecular mass, so the difference is entirely one of **shape**. A straight chain has a large surface area and its molecules can lie alongside one another, giving strong van der Waals forces; branching makes the molecule more compact and nearly spherical, reducing the surface of contact (Fig. 15.4). 2,2-Dimethylpropane is the most branched and boils lowest, and unbranched pentane boils highest.

[Textbook misprint: sub-item (b) is printed "but-l-ene", with a lowercase letter l where the digit 1 belongs. This is settled by the PDF's own character encoding rather than by the shape of the glyph: that character extracts as U+006C (lowercase L), while every genuine digit 1 on the same page — the block number, the 1 of "1 - chloropropane" and the 1 of \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\) — extracts as U+0031. The compound intended is but-1-ene, and the answer below is given for it; there is no such compound as "but-l-ene". Nothing else in the question is affected.]

Cold concentrated sulphuric acid **adds across the double bond according to Markovnikov's rule** to give an alkyl hydrogen sulfate; the chapter then says that when this alkyl hydrogen sulfate is diluted with water and heated, an alcohol with the same alkyl group is obtained. So the two steps together convert the alkene into the Markovnikov alcohol.

**a. Propene**

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H_2SO_4}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OSO_3H)-CH_3}\) (isopropyl hydrogen sulfate)

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OSO_3H)-CH_3 + H_2O}\) \(\xrightarrow{\Delta}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3 + H_2SO_4}\)

Product: **propan-2-ol** (isopropyl alcohol).

**b. But-1-ene**

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH=CH_2 + H_2SO_4}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(OSO_3H)-CH_3}\)

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(OSO_3H)-CH_3 + H_2O}\) \(\xrightarrow{\Delta}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(OH)-CH_3 + H_2SO_4}\)

Product: **butan-2-ol**.

In both cases the \(\mathrm{-OSO_3H}\) group, and therefore the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group, goes to the carbon carrying fewer hydrogen atoms — which is why, as the chapter's own "Can you tell?" box asks, propan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol cannot be made this way.

**a. From ethyl bromide — reduction by nascent hydrogen**

Zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid supply nascent hydrogen, which reduces the alkyl halide to the alkane:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Br + 2[H]}\) \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Zn,\ HCl}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_3 + HBr}\)

(ethyl bromide \(\rightarrow\) ethane). Note that the carbon skeleton is unchanged — the bromine is simply replaced by hydrogen.

**b. From ethyl magnesium iodide — hydrolysis of a Grignard reagent**

An alkyl magnesium halide on treatment with water gives the alkane:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Mg-I + H-O-H}\) \(\xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_3 + MgI(OH)}\)

(ethyl magnesium iodide \(\rightarrow\) ethane). Again one carbon-magnesium bond is replaced by a carbon-hydrogen bond, so the two-carbon skeleton is retained. Both are the chapter's own methods of preparing alkanes from alkyl halides, written here for the two-carbon case.

One monochlorination product arises from each **distinct kind** of hydrogen in the molecule, so the count is the number of different hydrogen environments.

**a. 2-Methylpropane, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CH}\) — 2 products**

All nine hydrogens of the three methyl groups are equivalent (each methyl is attached to the same central carbon), and there is one tertiary hydrogen on that central carbon.

| Hydrogen replaced | Product | IUPAC name |
|---|---|---|
| one of the nine primary H | \(\mathrm{ClCH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_3}\) | 1-Chloro-2-methylpropane |
| the tertiary H | \(\mathrm{CH_3-CCl(CH_3)-CH_3}\) | 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane |

**b. 2-Methylbutane, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3}\) — 4 products**

The two methyl groups on C-2 are equivalent to each other, so this molecule has four hydrogen environments: those two methyls, the tertiary C-2 hydrogen, the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) at C-3, and the terminal methyl at C-4.

| Hydrogen replaced | Product | IUPAC name |
|---|---|---|
| a C-2 methyl | \(\mathrm{ClCH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3}\) | 1-Chloro-2-methylbutane |
| the tertiary C-2 H | \(\mathrm{CH_3-CCl(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3}\) | 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane |
| a C-3 H | \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CHCl-CH_3}\) | 2-Chloro-3-methylbutane |
| a C-4 H | \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2Cl}\) | 1-Chloro-3-methylbutane |

The four are not formed in equal amounts: this chapter gives the ease of replacement of hydrogen as tertiary > secondary > primary, so the tertiary product is favoured relative to the number of hydrogens available.

Pyrolysis (cracking) is defined in this chapter as the decomposition of an alkane on heating to a high temperature **in the absence of air**, giving lower alkanes, alkenes and hydrogen. The chapter's own example breaks \(\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}\) three different ways, and butane behaves the same way — the \(\mathrm{C-C}\) and \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds break at different places, so a mixture is obtained:

\(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\) \(\xrightarrow{\Delta}\) \(\mathrm{C_4H_8 + H_2}\)  (butene + hydrogen)

\(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\) \(\xrightarrow{\Delta}\) \(\mathrm{C_3H_6 + CH_4}\)  (propene + methane)

\(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\) \(\xrightarrow{\Delta}\) \(\mathrm{C_2H_4 + C_2H_6}\)  (ethene + ethane)

Each split conserves all four carbon atoms and all ten hydrogen atoms, which is the check that no product has been invented or lost. So the possible products are **butene, propene, ethene, ethane, methane and hydrogen**.

Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism requires a carbon-carbon double bond in which **each** of the two doubly bonded carbons carries two *different* groups. If either carbon carries two identical groups, swapping them gives back the same molecule, so no separate isomer exists.

**a.** \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C(=CH_2)-CH_3}\) — the terminal carbon of the double bond is \(\mathrm{=CH_2}\) and carries **two hydrogens**, which are identical. No geometrical isomerism.

**b.** \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH_2}\) — worse still: one carbon carries two methyl groups and the other two hydrogens. Both ends are symmetrical, so no geometrical isomerism.

**c.** \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(C_2H_5)=C(C_2H_5)-CH_3}\) — each doubly bonded carbon carries a methyl group **and** an ethyl group, which are different from each other. This compound therefore **does exhibit geometrical isomerism**, existing as a cis form (the two methyls on the same side of the double bond) and a trans form (on opposite sides). Its IUPAC name is 3,4-dimethylhex-3-ene.

So only compound **c** shows geometrical isomerism.

Ethyl iodide is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-I}\). The two reagents take it in opposite directions — one removes HI, the other replaces the iodine by hydrogen.

**a. Alcoholic KOH — dehydrohalogenation (elimination), giving an alkene.**

On boiling with a hot concentrated alcoholic solution of KOH, iodine leaves the \(\alpha\)-carbon and a hydrogen leaves the adjacent \(\beta\)-carbon, so \(\mathrm{HI}\) is eliminated:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-I + KOH\ (alcoholic)}\) \(\xrightarrow{\text{boil}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH_2 + KI + H_2O}\)

The product is **ethene**. This is the chapter's own \(\beta\)-elimination example, written for the iodide instead of the bromide.

**b. Zn and HCl — reduction, giving an alkane.**

Zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid supply nascent hydrogen, which replaces the halogen:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-I + 2[H]}\) \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Zn,\ HCl}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_3 + HI}\)

The product is **ethane**. Note that both reactions keep the two-carbon skeleton intact; only the degree of saturation changes.

Ozonolysis cleaves the \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond and puts a carbonyl group on **each** of the two originally doubly bonded carbons. To find the alkene, do the reverse: take the two carbonyl compounds obtained and join their carbonyl carbons by a double bond.

Here both fragments are ethanal, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO}\). Joining the two carbonyl carbons gives

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\)

Counting checks the reconstruction: two \(\mathrm{C_2}\) fragments must rebuild a \(\mathrm{C_4}\) alkene, which this is.

The reaction run forwards confirms it:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\) \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{CCl_4}]{\mathrm{O_3}}\) ozonide \(\xrightarrow[\text{Zn dust}]{\mathrm{H_2O}}\) \(\mathrm{2\ CH_3-CHO}\)

**Structure:** \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\); **IUPAC name: but-2-ene.**

(Each doubly bonded carbon carries one hydrogen, which is why both fragments come out as an aldehyde rather than a ketone.)

Reverse the ozonolysis: join the carbonyl carbons of the two products by a double bond, replacing the two \(\mathrm{C=O}\) groups with one \(\mathrm{C=C}\).

Acetone is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\) (three carbons, the carbonyl carbon carrying two methyls) and acetaldehyde is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO}\) (two carbons, its carbonyl carbon carrying a methyl and a hydrogen). Joining them gives

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH-CH_3}\)

The carbon count checks out: a \(\mathrm{C_3}\) fragment plus a \(\mathrm{C_2}\) fragment must rebuild a \(\mathrm{C_5}\) alkene, which this is \((\mathrm{C_5H_{10}})\).

Run forwards:

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH-CH_3}\) \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{CCl_4}]{\mathrm{O_3}}\) ozonide \(\xrightarrow[\text{Zn dust}]{\mathrm{H_2O}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3 + CH_3-CHO}\)

**Structural formula:** \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)=CH-CH_3}\); **IUPAC name: 2-methylbut-2-ene.**

The ketone fragment tells us that one alkene carbon carried two alkyl groups, and the aldehyde fragment that the other carried one alkyl group and one hydrogen — which is exactly this structure.

[Textbook misprint: two alcohol names are misspelt in this question. Sub-item (a) is printed "nypropylalcohol", intended as n-propyl alcohol (propan-1-ol), and sub-item (b) is printed "isoproyl alcohol", intended as isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol). Both are answered below under their correct names. The two products are genuinely different compounds, so the question is only answerable once the names are read correctly.]

Both conversions add water across the double bond of propene; they differ in **which** carbon takes the \(\mathrm{-OH}\), so two different reagent systems are needed.

**a. Propene to n-propyl alcohol (propan-1-ol) — hydroboration-oxidation.**

The \(\mathrm{-OH}\) must go to the *terminal* carbon, which is the anti-Markovnikov position, so acid-catalysed hydration will not do. This chapter's hydroboration-oxidation gives exactly this: the alkene reacts with diborane in THF to form a trialkylborane, which on oxidation with alkaline hydrogen peroxide gives the primary alcohol.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2}\) \(\xrightarrow[\text{THF}]{(\mathrm{BH_3})_2}\) \(\mathrm{(CH_3-CH_2-CH_2)_3B}\) \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{NaOH}]{\mathrm{H_2O_2}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\)

**b. Propene to isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol) — acid-catalysed hydration.**

Here the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) goes to the middle carbon, which is the Markovnikov position, so direct hydration in the presence of an acid is used:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H-OH}\) \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

Equivalently, and as the chapter also shows, propene may be treated with cold concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) to give isopropyl hydrogen sulfate, which on dilution with water and heating gives propan-2-ol.

The contrast is the point of the question: the same alkene and the same overall addition of water give the primary alcohol by the anti-Markovnikov route and the secondary alcohol by the Markovnikov route.

But-2-ene is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\). The two permanganate reagents differ in strength: the cold dilute alkaline reagent only *hydroxylates* the double bond, while the acidic reagent *cleaves* it.

**a. Dilute alkaline \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) (Baeyer's reagent) — hydroxylation.**

Two \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups add across the double bond to give a vicinal diol (glycol), and the purple colour of \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) disappears:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\) \(\xrightarrow[\text{cold}]{\text{dil. alk. }\mathrm{KMnO_4}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

Product: **butane-2,3-diol**. This chapter notes that the discharge of the purple colour is used as a qualitative test for a double bond — **Baeyer's test**.

**b. Acidic \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) — oxidative cleavage.**

The chapter states that alkenes on oxidation with acidic \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) form ketones and/or acids. Each doubly bonded carbon of but-2-ene carries one hydrogen and one methyl group, so each fragment is oxidised to a carboxylic acid:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\) \(\xrightarrow[(\mathrm{O})]{\mathrm{KMnO_4,\ H^+}}\) \(\mathrm{2\ CH_3-COOH}\)

Product: **two moles of ethanoic acid (acetic acid)**. Because the molecule is symmetrical about the double bond, both halves give the same acid, and all four carbons are accounted for.

This is the chapter's route to a higher alkyne from a smaller terminal alkyne, followed by an addition.

**Step 1 — \(\mathrm{LiNH_2}\).** Lithium amide is a very strong base and removes the acidic terminal hydrogen of ethyne:

\(\mathrm{H-C \equiv C-H + Li^+NH_2^-}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{H-C \equiv C-Li + NH_3}\)

**A = ethynyllithium (lithium acetylide), \(\mathrm{HC \equiv C-Li}\).**

**Step 2 — \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl}\).** The acetylide attacks the primary alkyl halide, extending the chain:

\(\mathrm{H-C \equiv C-Li + CH_3CH_2Cl}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{H-C \equiv C-CH_2-CH_3 + LiCl}\)

**B = but-1-yne, \(\mathrm{HC \equiv C-CH_2CH_3}\).**

**Step 3 — HBr.** Hydrogen bromide adds across the triple bond according to Markovnikov's rule, the bromine going to the carbon carrying fewer hydrogens (compare the chapter's own propyne \(\rightarrow\) 2-bromopropene):

\(\mathrm{HC \equiv C-CH_2CH_3 + HBr}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{CH_2=CBr-CH_2CH_3}\)

**C = 2-bromobut-1-ene.** (With a second molecule of HBr the addition continues, again by Markovnikov's rule, to the geminal dihalide 2,2-dibromobutane.)

**Comment on the acidic nature of B.** B is but-1-yne, a **terminal** alkyne — its hydrogen is attached directly to an sp hybridised carbon. An sp hybrid orbital has 50% s-character, so the electrons are held tightly and close to the nucleus, making the sp carbon more electronegative than the \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) carbon of an alkene or the \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) carbon of an alkane. That hydrogen can therefore be given away as a proton to a very strong base, so **B is acidic**, in the same way and for the same reason as the ethyne it was made from — it would itself react with lithium amide to form an alkyn-1-yl lithium.

**a. From sodium benzoate — decarboxylation.**

Anhydrous sodium benzoate heated with soda-lime (NaOH with CaO) loses its carboxyl group as carbonate:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COONa + NaOH}\) \(\xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{CaO}}\) \(\mathrm{C_6H_6 + Na_2CO_3}\)

The equation balances as written: 7 carbons on the left (6 in the ring plus the carboxyl carbon) give 6 in benzene and 1 in \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\); both sodium atoms end up in the carbonate.

**b. From phenol — reduction.**

Vapours of phenol passed over heated zinc dust give benzene, the zinc taking the oxygen:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH + Zn}\) \(\xrightarrow{\Delta}\) \(\mathrm{C_6H_6 + ZnO}\)

Here the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group is replaced by \(\mathrm{-H}\); the single oxygen of phenol is removed as zinc oxide, so the equation balances with one zinc atom.

Each of these is an electrophilic substitution on a **mono**substituted benzene, so the position of the incoming group is decided by the group already on the ring, not by the incoming group. This chapter lists \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), \(\mathrm{-Br}\), \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\) and R as ortho/para directing, and \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) as meta directing and deactivating.

**a. Chlorination of nitrobenzene.** \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) is meta directing — the chapter's resonance structures show the ortho and para positions of nitrobenzene carry *less* electron density than the meta positions, so the electrophile \(\mathrm{Cl^{\oplus}}\) attacks meta. Product: **m-chloronitrobenzene** (1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene). \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) is also deactivating, so more vigorous conditions are needed than for benzene itself.

**b. Sulfonation of chlorobenzene.** \(\mathrm{-Cl}\) is ortho/para directing (though moderately deactivating through its \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect). Products: **o-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid and p-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid**, the para isomer predominating because the ortho positions are crowded by the chlorine.

**c. Bromination of phenol.** \(\mathrm{-OH}\) is strongly activating and ortho/para directing — the chapter's resonance structures of phenol show extra electron density at exactly those positions. Products: **o-bromophenol and p-bromophenol**. Because the ring is so strongly activated, an excess of bromine substitutes all the available ortho and para positions to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

**d. Nitration of toluene.** \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) is activating and ortho/para directing. Products: **o-nitrotoluene and p-nitrotoluene**, again with the para isomer as the major product.

This is **combustion**. The chapter states that alkanes heated in the presence of air or dioxygen are completely oxidised to carbon dioxide and water with the evolution of a large amount of heat, which is why alkanes are good fuels. Its general equation is

\(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2} + \dfrac{3n+1}{2}\ O_2}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{n\ CO_2 + (n+1)\ H_2O + \text{heat}}\)

For propane, \(n = 3\), so \(\dfrac{3(3)+1}{2} = 5\):

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_3 + 5\ O_2}\) \(\xrightarrow{\Delta}\) \(\mathrm{3\ CO_2 + 4\ H_2O}\)

The equation balances atom for atom: 3 C, 8 H and 10 O on each side. The main products are therefore **carbon dioxide and water** (with heat). If the supply of oxygen is limited the combustion is incomplete and poisonous carbon monoxide is formed instead, as the chapter's "Can you recall?" box points out.

This is **acid-catalysed dehydration of an alcohol**, one of this chapter's methods of preparing alkenes. The chapter notes that the exact conditions depend on the class of alcohol, and it uses **60% \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at 373 K for a secondary alcohol** — exactly the conditions printed here. Propan-2-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3}\), is a secondary alcohol.

The \(\mathrm{-OH}\) leaves from the \(\alpha\)-carbon together with a hydrogen from a \(\beta\)-carbon:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3}\) \(\xrightarrow[373\ \mathrm{K}]{60\%\ \mathrm{H_2SO_4}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H_2O}\)

The main product is **propene**. Unlike the chapter's butan-2-ol example, which gives a major and a minor alkene, propan-2-ol gives only one product: both of its \(\beta\)-carbons are identical methyl groups, so removing a hydrogen from either one leads to the same alkene.

\(\mathrm{H_2}\) over **Pd-C partially deactivated with quinoline is Lindlar's catalyst**. As this chapter explains, it reduces the triple bond only **partially**: a calculated quantity of dihydrogen converts \(\mathrm{C \equiv C}\) to \(\mathrm{C=C}\) and the reaction stops at the alkene instead of running on to the alkane, the two hydrogens adding to the same face so that a cis alkene is obtained.

\(\mathrm{HC \equiv C-CH_3 + H_2}\) \(\xrightarrow[\text{Pd-C/quinoline}]{}\) \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH_3}\)

The main product is **propene** (prop-1-ene).

The cis/trans distinction does not arise here: propyne is a *terminal* alkyne, so one of the alkene carbons ends up carrying two hydrogens and only one geometrical form of the product exists. (Had the catalyst been ordinary Pt, Pd or Ni with excess hydrogen, reduction would have gone all the way to propane.)

[Textbook misprint: the substrate of sub-item (d) is printed as \(\mathrm{H-C-H}\), which is not a possible structure — that carbon is shown with only two bonds, whereas carbon is tetravalent. The reagents identify what was intended: dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) containing 1 per cent \(\mathrm{HgSO_4}\) is the reagent this chapter uses for the hydration of alkynes, and the smallest alkyne, ethyne, is written \(\mathrm{H-C \equiv C-H}\). The triple bond has evidently dropped out in printing, leaving two plain hyphens. Verified on the rendered page at 8x magnification: two plain hyphens, no triple-bond glyph — while sub-item (c) of the same question prints its triple bond correctly, so the loss is local to this item. The answer below is given for ethyne.]

Ethyne adds a molecule of water in the presence of dilute sulphuric acid and mercuric sulphate. The unstable enol formed first rearranges at once to a carbonyl compound:

\(\mathrm{HC \equiv CH + H_2O}\) \(\xrightarrow[1\%\ \mathrm{HgSO_4}]{40\%\ \mathrm{H_2SO_4}}\) \(\mathrm{[CH_2=CH-OH]}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO}\)

The main product is **ethanal (acetaldehyde)**. Ethyne is the one alkyne that gives an aldehyde by this reaction; every higher alkyne, adding water by Markovnikov's rule, gives a ketone instead.

The product printed is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2Br}\).

To name it, take the longest chain containing the \(\mathrm{-CH_2Br}\) carbon: \(\mathrm{BrCH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_3}\) is a three-carbon chain (propane) carrying a bromine and a methyl group. Numbering from the end nearer the bromine puts \(\mathrm{Br}\) on C-1 and the methyl on C-2.

IUPAC name: **1-bromo-2-methylpropane**.

Note where the bromine has gone. The alkene was \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)=CH_2}\), whose terminal \(\mathrm{=CH_2}\) carbon carries **more** hydrogens; the bromine has added to that carbon, not to the more substituted one. That is the anti-Markovnikov orientation, and it is the point of part (b).

The rule is the **anti-Markovnikov rule, also called the peroxide effect or the Kharasch-Mayo effect**.

This chapter states that Kharasch and Mayo discovered in 1933 that the addition of HBr to an unsymmetrical alkene **in the presence of an organic peroxide** (here benzoyl peroxide, \(\mathrm{R-O-O-R}\)) takes place opposite to the orientation suggested by Markovnikov's rule: the bromine attaches to the carbon carrying the **greater** number of hydrogen atoms, and the hydrogen to the carbon carrying fewer.

That is what has happened here. Markovnikov addition to \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)=CH_2}\) would have put the bromine on the fully substituted carbon and given 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; with benzoyl peroxide present the bromine goes instead to the terminal \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), giving 1-bromo-2-methylpropane.

Two limits of the rule that this chapter notes are worth remembering: the effect is shown by **HBr only** — peroxide has no such effect on the addition of HCl or HI — and the alkene must be unsymmetrical, or the question of orientation does not arise.

**Step 1 — \(\mathrm{Br_2/CCl_4}\), room temperature.** Halogen adds across the double bond of the alkene to give a vicinal dihalide (two halogens on adjacent carbons). Carbon tetrachloride is the inert solvent; the reddish-brown colour of bromine is discharged, which is the chapter's test for unsaturation.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2 + Br_2}\) \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CCl_4}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_2Br}\)

**A = 1,2-dibromopropane.**

**Step 2 — Zn.** Zinc removes the two halogen atoms from adjacent carbons — dehalogenation — regenerating the double bond. This is the chapter's method of preparing alkenes from vicinal dihalides.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_2Br + Zn}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2 + ZnBr_2}\)

**B = propene.**

**Step 3 — dilute alkaline \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\).** This is Baeyer's reagent, which hydroxylates the double bond to a vicinal diol (glycol) while its purple colour disappears.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2}\) \(\xrightarrow[\text{cold}]{\text{dil. alk. }\mathrm{KMnO_4}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2OH}\)

**C = propane-1,2-diol** (propylene glycol).

The sequence is worth reading as a whole: steps 1 and 2 take the double bond away and put it back, so B is the same compound as the starting material, and only step 3 changes the molecule permanently.

This chapter gives three tests for aromaticity, all of which must be satisfied: the compound must be **cyclic and planar** with every ring atom \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridised; **every ring atom must carry a p-orbital**, and those p-orbitals must be parallel so that overlap is continuous around the ring; and the delocalised system must contain \((4n+2)\ \pi\) electrons with \(n\) an integer (Huckel's rule).

**A. Cyclopenta-1,3-diene — NOT aromatic.** The five-membered ring has two double bonds, so four \(\pi\) electrons; \(4n+2 = 4\) gives \(n = \tfrac{1}{2}\), which is not an integer. Independently of that, the fifth carbon is a \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group: it is \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridised and has no p-orbital, so the overlap is broken at that atom and delocalisation cannot run right around the ring. This is exactly the reason the chapter gives for cycloheptatriene being non-aromatic.

**B. Cyclobutadiene — NOT aromatic.** The four-membered ring is cyclic and planar and each carbon is \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) with a p-orbital, so the first two conditions are met — but its two double bonds give only four \(\pi\) electrons, and \(4n+2 = 4\) again requires \(n = \tfrac{1}{2}\). Huckel's rule fails, so the compound is not aromatic.

**C. Benzene — AROMATIC.** Worked out in this chapter: it is cyclic and planar, has a p-orbital on each carbon of the hexagonal ring so that continuous overlap above and below the ring is possible, and its three double bonds give six \(\pi\) electrons. \(4n + 2 = 6\), so \(4n = 4\) and \(n = 1\), an integer.

**D. Pyridine — AROMATIC.** Also worked out in this chapter. It has three double bonds and six \(\pi\) electrons in six parallel p-orbitals forming a delocalised \(\pi\) molecular orbital; \(4n+2 = 6\) gives \(n = 1\), an integer. The nitrogen's lone pair does **not** count, because it occupies an \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybrid orbital lying in the plane of the ring, not the p-orbital, and so takes no part in the delocalisation.

So C and D are aromatic; A and B are not.

The two reagents this chapter uses for the Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene are

1. **an acyl halide** — for example acetyl chloride, \(\mathrm{CH_3COCl}\), and
2. **an acid anhydride** — for example acetic anhydride, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\).

In either case benzene is heated with the reagent in the presence of **anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\)**, which is the catalyst rather than the acylating reagent itself:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl}\) \(\xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\text{anhy. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}}\) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl}\)

\(\mathrm{C_6H_6 + (CH_3CO)_2O}\) \(\xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\text{anhy. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}}\) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3 + CH_3COOH}\)

Both give 1-phenylethanone (acetophenone). The attacking species in each case is the **acylium ion**, \(\mathrm{R-C^{\oplus}=O}\).

The reaction is **Friedel-Crafts alkylation**.

A hydrogen atom of the benzene ring is replaced by an alkyl group — here the methyl group of methyl chloride — in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride, and the product is methylbenzene (toluene) with hydrogen chloride as the by-product. It is an example of the electrophilic substitution reactions that characterise aromatic compounds, and this chapter notes that it is the reaction used to extend a carbon chain outside the benzene ring.

(It is *alkylation* rather than *acylation* because the group introduced is \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), an alkyl group; acylation would introduce \(\mathrm{-COR}\) from an acyl chloride or an anhydride.)

The electrophile is the **methyl carbocation, \(\mathrm{CH_3^{\oplus}}\)** — the alkyl carbocation \(\mathrm{R^{\oplus}}\) that this chapter names as the electrophile of Friedel-Crafts alkylation.

Neither the benzene nor the methyl chloride attacks the ring as it stands: benzene is the electron-rich species, so the ring must be attacked by an electron-deficient one. The methyl chloride supplies that species only after the catalyst has pulled the chlorine away, leaving the methyl group short of a pair of electrons and therefore positively charged. It is this \(\mathrm{CH_3^{\oplus}}\) that bonds to a ring carbon, displacing a hydrogen as \(\mathrm{H^+}\) and giving toluene.

The electrophile is generated by the **anhydrous aluminium chloride**, which acts as a Lewis acid. \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) is electron-deficient — aluminium has only six electrons around it — so it accepts the lone pair of the chlorine of methyl chloride. The carbon-chlorine bond breaks heterolytically, the chlorine leaving with both bonding electrons as part of the tetrachloroaluminate ion and the methyl group leaving as a carbocation:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-Cl + AlCl_3}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{CH_3^{\oplus} + [AlCl_4]^-}\)

This chapter writes the general step as \(\mathrm{R-Cl + AlCl_3 \longrightarrow R^{\oplus} + AlCl_4^-}\).

Two points follow. The catalyst must be **anhydrous**: any water would destroy \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) and no carbocation would be produced. And the \(\mathrm{[AlCl_4]^-}\) formed here is what later removes the \(\mathrm{H^+}\) from the ring to restore aromaticity, releasing \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and regenerating the \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) — which is why the aluminium chloride is a catalyst rather than a reactant consumed in the reaction.
